title: SHORT-TERM GAINS, LONG-TERM GAPS: THE IMPACT OF GENAI AND SEARCH TECHNOLOGIES ON RETENTION
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether different information tools—Generative AI (ChatGPT), a search engine (Google), an e-textbook, or no tool—affect students’ immediate learning performance and later retention across tasks of different cognitive complexity. The study is motivated by concern that AI tools may improve short-term task completion by providing fast, structured answers, but may not support durable learning or higher-order thinking. Using Bloom’s taxonomy, the authors compare effects across lower-order tasks (remembering/understanding), medium-order tasks (applying), and higher-order tasks (analyzing/evaluating/creating).

The intervention was an experimentally controlled comparison of four conditions. Students were randomly assigned to a control group, an e-textbook group, a Google group, or a ChatGPT group. All participants completed three sequential data-privacy learning tasks and then took corresponding quizzes without access to external tools. A delayed post-test administered three weeks after the final task measured retention. The study therefore evaluates both immediate achievement and longer-term retention under different technology conditions.

The population consisted of 123 students from an information systems department at a private university, and the study was conducted in a supervised laboratory setting as part of a course context. Lecture/demonstration sessions preceded the lab activities, and the lab sessions restricted students to only their assigned resource. The topic domain was data privacy and GDPR, and tasks were scenario-based and aligned to Bloom’s revised taxonomy.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT and Google improved immediate performance on lower- and medium-complexity tasks relative to the control group, especially for remembering, understanding, and applying. However, these advantages weakened over time: retention scores for ChatGPT and Google declined and converged with other groups, and no significant advantage appeared for higher-order tasks. For the most complex task, no significant group differences were found, and the control group showed the highest retention. The authors argue that AI and search tools can support efficient short-term performance, but do not automatically promote long-term retention or deeper cognition unless paired with structured pedagogical strategies.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot that produces natural-language responses and synthesized information to user prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Students in the ChatGPT condition used only ChatGPT to complete three data-privacy learning tasks spanning Bloom's taxonomy levels (remember/understand, apply, analyze/evaluate/create), and were then assessed immediately and again three weeks later without tool access.

findings.finding_summary: For the lower-order 'knowing and understanding' task, the ChatGPT group had the highest immediate assessment performance (M=82.6, SD=17.8) and significantly outperformed the e-textbook group and control group by mean differences of 16.60 and 22.39, respectively (p<.01). The univariate ANOVA for Task 1 was significant, F(3,119)=10.650, p<.001, partial η²=.212.
findings.measure: Immediate post-task assessment score for Task 1 (remembering and understanding)

findings.finding_summary: For the medium-complexity 'applying' task, the ChatGPT group again showed the best immediate performance (M=67.9, SD=20.0). The control group scored significantly lower than the ChatGPT group, with a mean difference of 20.15 (p<.01); the overall Task 2 ANOVA was F(3,119)=7.279, p<.001, partial η²=.155.
findings.measure: Immediate post-task assessment score for Task 2 (applying)

findings.finding_summary: For the higher-order task involving synthesizing, evaluating, and creating, the ChatGPT group did not differ significantly from other groups. Task 3 scores for the ChatGPT group were M=41.2, SD=14.8, and the overall ANOVA was not significant, F(3,119)=0.768, p=.514.
findings.measure: Immediate post-task assessment score for Task 3 (synthesizing, evaluating, creating)

findings.finding_summary: For Task 1 retention, the ChatGPT group's score dropped from the immediate assessment mean of 82.6 (SD=17.8) to a three-week retention mean of 65.5 (SD=22.1). The assessment-by-time interaction was significant, Wilk's λ=.885, F(3,119)=5.175, p<.01, partial η=.115, and the paper states that the ChatGPT group experienced a notable drop in retention scores.
findings.measure: Three-week retention score for Task 1 relative to immediate assessment

findings.finding_summary: For Task 2 retention, the ChatGPT group showed a small decline from immediate assessment (M=67.9, SD=20.0) to retention (M=64.5, SD=21.1), but the paper reports that none of the effects were statistically significant. Thus, ChatGPT did not produce a significant retention advantage for the applying task.
findings.measure: Three-week retention score for Task 2 relative to immediate assessment

findings.finding_summary: For Task 3 retention, the ChatGPT group's score declined slightly from M=41.2 (SD=14.8) to M=39.9 (SD=15.1), but no effects were statistically significant. The paper notes that the control group had the highest retention on this higher-order task.
findings.measure: Three-week retention score for Task 3 relative to immediate assessment

identified_tools.name: Google
identified_tools.description: Google's web search engine for retrieving online information through search queries.
identified_tools.use_case: Students in the Google condition used only the Google search engine to complete the same three data-privacy learning tasks, followed by immediate quizzes and a three-week retention test completed without tool access.

findings.finding_summary: For the lower-order 'knowing and understanding' task, the Google group scored M=79.1 (SD=17.4) and significantly outperformed the control group by a mean difference of 18.90 (p<.01). The overall Task 1 ANOVA was significant, F(3,119)=10.650, p<.001, partial η²=.212.
findings.measure: Immediate post-task assessment score for Task 1 (remembering and understanding)

findings.finding_summary: For the 'applying' task, the Google group scored M=66.6 (SD=13.7), and the control group scored significantly lower than the Google group by a mean difference of 18.81 (p<.01). The overall Task 2 ANOVA was significant, F(3,119)=7.279, p<.001, partial η²=.155.
findings.measure: Immediate post-task assessment score for Task 2 (applying)

findings.finding_summary: For the higher-order Task 3, the Google group had M=41.5 (SD=14.8), and there were no significant differences among groups. The overall ANOVA was F(3,119)=0.768, p=.514.
findings.measure: Immediate post-task assessment score for Task 3 (synthesizing, evaluating, creating)

findings.finding_summary: For Task 1 retention, the Google group's score declined from the immediate assessment mean of 79.1 (SD=17.4) to a three-week retention mean of 67.8 (SD=25.4). The assessment-by-time interaction for Task 1 was significant, Wilk's λ=.885, F(3,119)=5.175, p<.01, partial η=.115, and the paper notes that the Google group saw a decline, though less pronounced than ChatGPT.
findings.measure: Three-week retention score for Task 1 relative to immediate assessment

findings.finding_summary: For Task 2 retention, the Google group's score changed from M=66.6 (SD=13.7) to M=63.1 (SD=20.1), but the paper reports that none of the effects were statistically significant. This indicates no significant retention difference for the applying task.
findings.measure: Three-week retention score for Task 2 relative to immediate assessment

findings.finding_summary: For Task 3 retention, the Google group's mean declined from 41.5 (SD=14.8) to 40.6 (SD=13.8), but no effects were statistically significant. The study reports no significant retention differences across groups for this higher-order task.
findings.measure: Three-week retention score for Task 3 relative to immediate assessment

quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized experimental pre/post study with a control group and three comparison conditions, which is stronger than correlational evidence. However, it is a single-institution lab study with a modest sample (n=123), restricted-resource conditions, and some design limitations noted by the authors, so it does not reach blue-tier confidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports statistically significant immediate learning effects with moderate effect sizes at the task level (partial η²=.212 for Task 1 and .155 for Task 2), indicating meaningful short-term impact. However, retention benefits were weak or absent, so the impact is strong but concentrated in immediate performance rather than long-term learning.
